transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Hi. Um, well, I came in because I just can’t shake this heavy, hopeless feeling. It's like... like everything I built after the divorce has just completely collapsed, and I’m just sitting under it. Which is ironic, I guess, because I'm a civil engineer, so structural collapse is literally what I spend all day trying to prevent. 

Like, right now we're working on this retaining wall project out by the interstate, and the soil grading is a complete mess. I keep telling the contractors that if they don't stabilize the base, the whole slope is going to give way after the next heavy rain. They just nod and ignore me, which is exactly what my ex-husband used to do whenever I tried to talk about our finances or, you know, anything important. He actually bought a boat once without telling me. A boat! We lived two hours from the nearest lake. 

But... yeah, anyway. I just feel like I'm buried under all this rubble right now and I can't get out.
How long have you been feeling this heavy, hopeless way—did it start suddenly after the divorce, or has it been going on for months or longer?

Um, it’s been about a month, I think. It really started hanging over me right around the time all the financial mess from the divorce blew up. Which, honestly, was a total nightmare because we had to untangle all these joint accounts, and we used this local credit union where the online portal looks like it was coded in 1998. 

I remember trying to download our transaction history to prove he was using marital funds for the slip fees for that stupid boat—the slip fees! He was paying $400 a month to dock a boat we never even used! And the website wouldn't let me export to a spreadsheet, so I had to sit there and manually type it all out. I actually ended up calling their customer service, and the guy on the phone, I think his name was Gary, he kept asking if I wanted to upgrade to a platinum rewards card. Like, Gary, I am literally liquidating my life right now, I don't need two percent cash back on dining. 

But... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, the timeline. Yeah, so it's been about a month of feeling like this.
Over this past month, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy, even outside of the divorce stress?

Um... loss of interest? I guess... I mean, I don't really know if I've noticed that. It's hard to tell because I'm just so exhausted all the time. But speaking of things I used to enjoy, I used to love going to this little pottery studio downtown. It was right next to this amazing bakery that made the best sourdough croissants. Have you ever had a sourdough croissant? They are incredible. The baker, her name is Elise, she studied in Paris for like three years and she uses this starter that she's kept alive since she was in culinary school. She actually showed it to me once, it's in this massive glass jar in the back. 

But the pottery place, they closed down during the pandemic and never reopened. It's a shame, really, because the owner was this sweet older guy who always played jazz music while we worked. I made this really uneven, lopsided mug there once that I still use for my coffee at the office. My coworker, Dave, always makes fun of it. Dave is the guy who always leaves his lunch in the fridge until it turns into a science experiment. Last week, I had to throw away his Tupperware because it smelled like death. I don't understand how people can just be so oblivious to shared spaces, you know? Like, it's a communal fridge, Dave. 

But um... yeah, I'm not really sure about losing interest in things. I just haven't really been doing much of anything lately.
Would you say this heavy, hopeless feeling is with you most of the day, nearly every day, or does it mainly come up when something reminds you of the divorce?

Um, it's pretty much all the time. From the second I wake up, it's just... there. That heavy, hopeless feeling I mentioned before. It's like I'm trapped under all that rubble and I can't move, no matter what I'm doing. It doesn't even have to be about the divorce, it's just this constant weight. 

Speaking of weight, they actually had to bring in a specialized crane at the site yesterday to move these massive concrete barriers. The operator, this guy named Mike, he was telling me about how he used to work on oil rigs in the Gulf. He said the food out there was actually amazing, like they had steak and lobster on Fridays. Which is wild to me, because when I think of oil rigs, I just think of, like, rust and danger. My uncle actually worked on a rig for a few years, but he had to quit because he got terrible seasickness. He ended up opening a hardware store instead. He sells these really specific, imported brass hinges that are impossible to find anywhere else. 

But yeah, to answer your question... it's all day, every day. Just... stuck under it all.

Before the divorce and before this past month, would you say you've generally had a pattern—going back to your teens or twenties—of intense, unstable relationships or a shifting sense of who you are, or is this kind of emotional turmoil new for you?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I've always just kind of been me, you know? My twenties were pretty stable, mostly because I was just completely buried in engineering classes. Concrete design, fluid mechanics... actually, fluid mechanics was taught by this professor, Dr. Aris, who always wore these really loud, intensely patterned bow ties. Like, neon polka dots and bright zigzags. He said his wife made them for him, which is sweet, I guess, but they were so distracting when you were trying to learn about pipe friction. 

She owned a fabric store out in the suburbs, one of those places that smells heavily of lavender and dust. I went there once to buy felt for a presentation board, and they had this massive orange cat sleeping right on the cash register. It wouldn't even move when you tried to pay. You just had to kind of slide your credit card under its paw to reach the machine. The card reader was one of those really old, clunky ones with the buttons that stick. 

But um, wait, what was the question? Oh, the emotional turmoil and relationships. Yeah, no, this is all pretty new. Before the divorce, things were pretty normal and steady. I never really had any of that shifting identity stuff.
Over this past month, have you noticed any changes in your sleep—like trouble falling asleep, waking up in the middle of the night, or waking up much earlier than usual?

Yeah, my sleep has been... really bad. Lately I either just lie awake staring at the ceiling, replaying all my bills and every little mistake I've made at work, or... well, actually, speaking of the ceiling, while I was lying there the other night I noticed this weird water stain starting to form right near the air vent. It's shaped exactly like the state of Nevada. Which is kind of funny because my sister just moved to Nevada last year, out in Henderson. She says the heat there is just unbelievable. She had to buy these special thermal blackout curtains for her living room just to keep her AC from running all day. They're this really heavy, dark green velvet material, almost like what you'd see in an old movie theater. 

I actually used to do set design for my high school theater club. We did *The Music Man* my junior year, and I had to paint this massive backdrop of a town square. The paint we used was this cheap industrial stuff, and the fumes gave me the worst headache. Our drama teacher, Mr. Gable, was always trying to cut corners on the budget so he could afford better costumes. He was obsessed with getting these authentic 1910s boater hats for the barbershop quartet. 

But um... what were we talking about? Oh, sleep. Right. Yeah, if I'm not lying awake worrying about everything, I usually just end up waking up way before dawn anyway, and I just feel like I never actually slept at all.
Have you been having any thoughts that you're worthless or excessively guilty about things, or any thoughts of death or of not wanting to be alive?

Yeah, I mean... I just keep telling myself I'm a terrible engineer, a failed wife, just a complete burden to everyone. I just lie there and replay every missed calculation or every tense email I've sent, and it's just like proof that I ruin things. 

Actually, speaking of emails, our IT guy at work, Dave, just implemented this new email security protocol last week. It's supposed to stop phishing scams, but it's so aggressive that it keeps sending all my emails from the concrete suppliers straight to the spam folder. Dave is a nice guy, though. He breeds these tiny, expensive geckos in his spare time. He showed me a picture of one that was neon orange and blue. He keeps them in these elaborate glass terrariums with custom misting systems. 

My cousin actually tried to build a terrarium once for a pet snake he caught in the woods, but he didn't secure the lid right, and the snake got out and lived in his walls for like a month. They had to hire this guy who specialized in removing exotic pets to come find it. The guy used this weird thermal camera to track the snake's body heat behind the drywall. 

But um... yeah, what was I saying? Oh, right, just feeling like a failure. It's just this constant loop of guilt about everything I've ever messed up. As for thoughts of death... I don't know, it's just so heavy, I sometimes wonder if it would just be easier if I wasn't here, you know? Just to stop feeling so guilty all the time.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a one-month history of persistent, nearly constant depressed/hopeless mood, sleep disturbance (early waking, difficulty staying asleep), pervasive guilt and feelings of worthlessness/failure, fatigue, and passive suicidal ideation ('easier if I wasn't here'). These symptoms exceed the reactive, proportionate response expected in adjustment disorder and meet criteria for a major depressive episode of unspecified severity, with no history of manic/hypomanic episodes or longstanding personality instability (ruling out bipolar disorder or borderline personality disorder). Because this appears to be a single episode without prior psychiatric history, F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, unspecified) is most appropriate, though adjustment disorder with depressed mood and persistent depressive disorder remain considerations given the clear precipitating stressor (divorce) and need to clarify chronicity beyond one month.
